column6: You described learning in your organization as foundational: handled case by case, with limited shared processes. That is a common starting point, and a few simple, shared ways of working can make a visible difference quickly.

column6: You described your learning practice as established, with standard processes, ownership and reporting across most programs. The focus now is less on setting things up and more on where to direct effort.

column4: Content upkeep: Keeping existing learning content accurate, relevant and up to date.
column6: Identify your most-used and highest-risk content and review it first for outdated information, accessibility gaps and parts you could reuse. Give each item a review date so upkeep becomes routine.
column7: You named keeping content accurate and up to date as your main challenge.

column4: Delivery capacity: Producing and delivering learning fast enough to meet demand.
column6: Make demand visible in one backlog, agree how requests are prioritized, and build reusable templates and patterns so each new program takes less effort.
column7: You named delivering learning fast enough to meet demand as your main challenge.

column4: Learner engagement: Getting people to take part in learning and apply it at work.
column6: Design programs around the tasks people do at work, add practice and on-the-job support, and ask managers to reinforce what was learned.
column7: You named getting people to take part in learning and apply it as your main challenge.

column4: Consistent quality: Keeping quality consistent across programs, teams or regions.
column6: Agree a short quality checklist covering design, accuracy, accessibility and learner experience, and use it in every review, whoever builds the program.
column7: You named keeping quality consistent across programs, teams or regions as your main challenge.

column4: Demonstrating impact: Showing how learning contributes to business results.
column6: For one or two priority programs, agree with the business owner which operational measure the program should influence, capture a baseline, and plan how you will review the change.
column7: You named showing how learning contributes to business results as your main challenge.

column4: Delivery capacity: Increase delivery capacity.
column6: Look at where time goes today, from request to launch, and remove the biggest bottlenecks before adding more programs. Reusable designs and clear sign-off steps add capacity without adding people.
column7: You chose increasing delivery capacity as your goal for the next 6–12 months.

column4: Faster development: Reduce development and update time.
column6: Build a library of reusable templates, components and examples, and keep source files organized so updates are quicker to make.
column7: You chose reducing development and update time as your goal for the next 6–12 months.

column4: Quality and consistency: Improve learning quality and consistency.
column6: Define what good looks like for your programs, share it with everyone who builds or reviews learning, and check a sample of programs against it each quarter.
column7: You chose improving learning quality and consistency as your goal for the next 6–12 months.

column4: Engagement and application: Improve learner engagement and application.
column6: Choose one program and add practice, reminders and manager follow-up after it, then compare participation and feedback with earlier runs.
column7: You chose improving learner engagement and application as your goal for the next 6–12 months.

column4: Business impact: Demonstrate business impact.
column6: Choose a small number of programs where a business outcome can reasonably be linked to learning, and agree with stakeholders how results will be evaluated and reported.
column7: You chose demonstrating business impact as your goal for the next 6–12 months.

column4: Foundational: Learning is handled case by case, with limited shared processes.
column6: Set up one shared way to request, prioritize and track learning work, with a named owner for each program. Even a lightweight process makes demand visible and decisions easier.
column7: You said learning is handled case by case, so a shared process is the foundation the other priorities depend on.

column4: Developing: Some processes and tools are established, but consistency varies.
column6: Pick the processes and templates that work best today and make them the default for new programs, with a short checklist for design and review.
column7: You said consistency varies, so standardizing proven practices reduces rework without adding much overhead.

column4: Established: Standard processes, ownership, and reporting are in place across most programs.
column6: Review your portfolio against current business priorities, and retire or refresh programs that no longer earn their place. Use your existing reporting to decide where to invest.
column7: With standard processes and reporting in place, the biggest gains come from where you direct effort.

column4: Optimizing: Learning is aligned to business priorities and improved using evidence.
column6: Use the evidence you already collect to find the programs with the clearest results, and apply their design patterns more widely.
column7: You said learning is already improved using evidence, so the next step is to spread what works rather than add new process.

column4: In-person ILT: In-person instructor-led training (ILT).
column6: You deliver learning through in-person sessions. Consider which parts could be supported with short reference materials or follow-up activities, so learning continues after the session.

column4: Virtual ILT: Virtual instructor-led training (VILT).
column6: You deliver learning through virtual live sessions. Keep sessions interactive and focused, and add simple follow-up materials so people can revisit key points.

column4: Self-paced eLearning: Self-paced eLearning.
column6: You use self-paced eLearning. Review your most-used modules regularly for outdated examples and accessibility gaps, and look for content you could reuse across courses.

column4: Microlearning: Microlearning or performance support, such as short videos and job aids.
column6: You use microlearning and performance support. Make sure each resource is easy to find at the moment of need, and link related resources so they support a bigger goal.

column4: Reference materials: Documents or reference materials.
column6: You use documents and reference materials. Keep them current, easy to search and clearly owned, and consider which topics would benefit from practice or guided learning.

column4: Mainly partners: Mainly by external partners.
column6: As partners deliver most of the work, keep ownership of priorities, quality standards and final sign-off inside your organization.

column4: Content upkeep: Keeping existing learning content accurate, relevant and up to date.
column6: List your most-used learning assets and note when each was last reviewed. Pick the two most out of date and schedule their review.

column4: Delivery capacity: Producing and delivering learning fast enough to meet demand.
column6: Put every open learning request into one list with a requester, a deadline and a business reason, and agree the top priorities with stakeholders.

column4: Learner engagement: Getting people to take part in learning and apply it at work.
column6: Ask a few recent participants and their managers what they have used at work since the program, and note what got in the way.

column4: Consistent quality: Keeping quality consistent across programs, teams or regions.
column6: Draft a one-page quality checklist and test it on two recent programs, ideally built by different people or partners.

column4: Demonstrating impact: Showing how learning contributes to business results.
column6: Pick one priority program and agree with its business owner which measure it should influence and where the data will come from.

column4: Delivery capacity: Increase delivery capacity.
column6: Map how a typical program moves from request to launch, remove the biggest bottleneck, and create reusable templates for your most common requests.

column4: Faster development: Reduce development and update time.
column6: Build a shared library of templates and reusable components, and organize source files so any program can be updated quickly.

column4: Quality and consistency: Improve learning quality and consistency.
